title: The true good
hookLine: the good belongs to reason, not to the senses (Letters 124)
last: PLAIN BREAD — HUNGER IS THE SAUCE.

cards: A puppy rolls in the grass in the sun. It's warm, fed, scratched behind the ears. Is it having a good life?
The obvious answer is yes. Letter 124 says something stranger. It's the last of Seneca's letters to Lucilius that survive, and he ends not with a goodbye but with an argument.
How do we know what's good? Do we feel it, the way the puppy feels the sun? Or do we understand it?
His answer sounds cold at first. Stay with it to the end.

teach.b: First, the question. The rival school of Epicurus said the good is pleasure, and pleasure is judged by the senses. Seneca disagrees.
The senses can tell you warm from cold, sweet from bitter. They can't tell you what's worth doing. That's the job of reason.

Second, the puppy and the baby. An animal, or an infant who can't yet reason, can be healthy, lively, comfortable. But the full good, in the Stoic sense, belongs only to a creature that can understand and choose.
He isn't saying the puppy doesn't matter.

teach.h: THE PUPPY'S GOOD AND A PERSON'S GOOD.
teach.b: Its kind of good is a different thing from the good of a person who chooses well. Third, why this frees you.

teach.h: GOOD THAT NO BAD NIGHT CAN TAKE.
teach.b: If the good were pleasure, anyone who controls your comfort would control your good. A bad night's sleep would ruin it. Seneca's good lives in reason, in what you choose to do with the night you got.
Fourth, the letters end mid-conversation. An ancient writer, Aulus Gellius, quotes from a later book of the letters, so there were once more. They're gone.
Seneca's last surviving word to his friend is an argument, still going. And our week, looking back: learn to live, try it, rich in enough, under the gold, with the sun, hunger is the sauce.
Every one of those is reason's good, chosen over what the senses wanted first.

how: Some Stoic practitioners pause before a choice to separate what the senses want from what reason judges good, following the teaching Seneca sets out in Letter 124.

s: Letter 124 is Seneca's goodbye to Lucilius
it's the last letter that survives, and it ends mid-argument; more once existed.
Seneca says the full good belongs to a creature that can reason
an animal or infant can be healthy, but the Stoic good is chosen.
he says their kind of good is different, not that they don't count.

games.q: you're an Epicurean arguing with Seneca. you say the good is pleasure, judged by the senses. what does he answer?
o: the senses can't judge what's worth doing; reason does.
games.why: Seneca says the senses report warm and sweet, but only reason can tell what is good.

practice: Think of one choice coming up where craving and reason pull different ways, another coffee or water, snapping back or waiting, and let craving speak first, fully.
Then let reason speak, slowly: what would you choose if you could see the whole day from the evening? You don't have to decide yet; just notice that you're the one who listens to both.

wordCard.voice: Ratio. Latin for reason: Seneca's last surviving letter says the true good lives not in what the senses feel, but in what reason understands and chooses. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, 'reason': where Seneca says the true good lives.

carryVoice: Your line: reason's good. It lives in what you choose, and no bad night can take it. Rest well.
